analysis.one_liner: Raises penalties on health plans that violate surprise-medical-billing protections.
analysis.headline: The bill had 38 cosponsors from both parties, but no House committee has held a markup or vote since its July 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal No Surprises Act already bars insurers from sticking patients with surprise out-of-network bills, but the penalty for breaking that rule is small — $100 a day — and enforcement has been limited. This bill raises the penalty to $10,000 per violation, adds a three-times penalty for insurers or providers that fail to pay what arbitration awards, and requires regulators to report to Congress twice a year on audits, complaints, and fines. It was referred to three House committees in July 2025 and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who get emergency care or scheduled treatment at an in-network hospital but are treated by an out-of-network doctor. Stronger penalties give insurers a real financial reason to follow the surprise-billing rules, and the new reports would show Congress and the public whether the agencies are actually enforcing them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients hit with surprise medical bills

how_it_helps.text: Raises the civil penalty for a plan or insurer that violates the surprise-billing protections to $10,000 per failure, up from $100 per day.

Adds a three-times payment penalty — plus interest — for a plan, insurer, or provider that misses or refuses the payment required after an arbitration (IDR) decision, and requires repayment within 30 days when a provider received more than the arbitration amount plus the patient's cost sharing.

Requires the health, labor, and treasury departments to report to Congress every six months on audits conducted, complaints from patients and providers, enforcement actions, penalties issued, and the most commonly reported violations.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer-sponsored group health plans that violate the rules would face fines of up to $10,000 per affected patient, and triple damages plus interest for late or missed arbitration payments. Some of those costs could be passed along through premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The new payment rules cut both ways: an out-of-network provider or facility that received an initial payment larger than the arbitration award must repay the difference within 30 days, and providers that pay late owe the same three-times penalty as insurers do.

The bill adds penalties and reporting requirements but no new funding for the agencies that would have to conduct the audits and collect the fines, so its effect depends on existing enforcement capacity.
Heavier penalty exposure for insurers and employer plans raises compliance costs, some portion of which is likely to show up in premiums or employer benefit costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefits are direct: surprise-billing protections become expensive for insurers to violate, and the six-month reports create public visibility into whether the rules are enforced. The costs — higher penalties for noncompliant plans and new repayment duties for providers — fall on parties that benefit from the status quo, though some may be passed to consumers through premiums. The main weakness is that the bill creates enforcement tools without funding the enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees in July 2025 and has had no hearings, markups, or floor vote since.

narrative.text: Representative Gregory Murphy (R-NC) introduced the bill on July 23, 2025, joined by five original cosponsors from both parties, including Jimmy Panetta (D-CA).
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and also to Education and Workforce and Ways and Means — a three-committee referral that means any one of them can hold it up.
The bill has 38 cosponsors: 21 of 223 House Republicans and 17 of 217 House Democrats.
No committee has taken further action since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, health insurers and employer plans are better off: the stricter penalties and payment rules are not in effect, and the bill is sitting without committee action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employer plans, for now

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Republican, and the 38 cosponsors split 21 Republicans to 17 Democrats; there has been no floor vote, so no partisan roll-call exists.

industries.note: The bill raises the fine for violating surprise-billing protections from $100 a day to $10,000 per failure and adds triple damages for late payment after arbitration. Insurers' interest in avoiding those penalties runs against patients' interest in the protections being enforced.
Self-insured employer plans face the same $10,000-per-affected-individual penalty under ERISA for balance-billing violations. Larger penalty exposure is a compliance cost for plan sponsors.

Providers gain a three-times payment penalty against plans that pay late or refuse an arbitration award, but must repay plans within 30 days when an award comes in below the initial payment plus patient cost sharing, and owe the same triple penalty if they pay late.

Air ambulance services are covered by the same arbitration and payment rules, so operators gain the triple penalty against late-paying plans and owe it themselves when they pay late or must return an overpayment.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to three committees with no movement in their first months never get a standalone vote, regardless of cosponsor count. Bipartisan, enforcement-focused health bills sometimes ride to passage attached to a larger health package, but with no scheduled committee action, the likely path is stalling in committee for the rest of this Congress.
